content.title: 5 Tips to Boost Your Chances of Seeing the Northern Lights
content.text: Credit: Philippe Bourseiller / Getty Images News Key Takeaways The northern lights are sometimes visible from the contiguous U.S., especially in recent years.The four key factors in seeing auroras are the strength of the solar storm, timing, location, and distance from light pollution.Your smartphone can help you see auroras that are too faint to identify with the naked eye. Seeing the northern lights always felt like a phenomenon you’d have to cross the ocean to somewhere like Iceland or Finland to experience—but if it seems like the northern lights have been a hotter topic of discussion in the U.S. lately, you’re not wrong. The solar maximum has now passed, meaning our chances of seeing dramatic auroras in lower latitudes like the contiguous U.S. have decreased compared to last year. However, strong solar flares that lead to coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and geomagnetic storms that result in impressive aurora displays remain likely for 2026, according to Space.com. If you want to improve your chances of seeing the northern lights in the U.S., there are some important facts to know. Key Factors Whether or not you’ll be able to see the northern lights will always come down to a handful of factors, as identified by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)'s Space Weather Prediction Center. 1. Geomagnetic Activity OK, now it's time for the science of it all: The level of geomagnetic activity of any given solar storm that could result in visible auroras is measured by its planetary K (Kp) index number, which will always range from 0 to 9. The lower the number, the less impressive the auroras. For the most part, you need to see a Kp of at least 6 to see visible auroras in the contiguous U.S. To see the latest space weather conditions and forecasts for the U.S., NOAA’s SWPC website always has up-to-date information both on its homepage and on its aurora dashboard. Aurora tracking apps like My Aurora Forecast & Alerts are also helpful tools. 2. Location The farther north you are, the better. This, of course, is good news for northern states, which will always have the best chances of seeing visible auroras—and that’s why Alaska is such a hotbed for northern lights activity. No matter where you are, you’ll want to have a clear view of the northern horizon for the best chance of seeing an aurora, according to the NOAA. Related 3. Dark Skies The best time to see the northern lights is at night, and the most dramatic displays will be visible away from the light pollution of cities, the NOAA notes. This same advice, of course, will also prove helpful if you’re trying to see a meteor shower or do any other sort of stargazing. For the very best shot at viewing the northern lights or any sky phenomena, you can head to a certified dark sky location identified by DarkSky International. The U.S. is home to over 150 certified dark sky sites. 4. Timing Auroras can be incredibly difficult to predict, but they are generally most visible between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m. local time, according to NOAA. And the best times of year for viewing auroras tend to be around the spring and fall equinoxes. 5. Your Phone While NOAA didn’t include this particular tip, we’d also note that your phone can be a helpful tool for picking up auroras that are too faint to be seen with the naked eye. Using an iPhone, for example, enable Night Mode, turn off your flash, set a 5-15 second exposure, and use a tripod (if you have one) for best results.
